sourceBindings.text: A plant needs 17 essential elements to complete its life cycle. Carbon (C), hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) make up much of its mass and come chiefly from air and water. The other essential elements are obtained mainly as mineral nutrients through the growing medium. None of the essentials can simply be ignored because another is plentiful.

Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) are called the three primary mineral macronutrients. Calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and sulfur (S) are also mineral macronutrients, often called secondary macronutrients. The eight essential micronutrients are iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), boron (B), molybdenum (Mo), chlorine (Cl) and nickel (Ni). Together with C, H and O, these make the 17 essentials. Calling N–P–K 'the big three' concerns common mineral fertilizer needs; it does not mean these three exceed C, H and O in total plant mass or that every field needs all three added.

A soil can contain a nutrient yet supply too little of it to a root at a particular time. Roots mostly take up dissolved nutrient ions from the soil solution. Water, pH, the way nutrients bind to soil particles, microbial activity and root conditions affect availability. Soil analysis and the crop context matter before choosing a fertilizer.

sourceBindings.text: Nitrogen is N. Roots commonly take it up as nitrate (NO₃⁻) or ammonium (NH₄⁺). Phosphorus is P. In ordinary agricultural soil solution, its principal phosphate uptake forms are H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻; their relative amounts depend on pH. Potassium is K and is taken up as K⁺. These are ions in solution, not loose pieces of solid N, P or K entering a root.

PO₄³⁻ is not a principal uptake form under ordinary agricultural soil conditions. The common phosphate uptake forms discussed here are H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻. Detailed transport to roots follows in the step “Nutrient transport to roots and within plants”.

sourceBindings.text: Imagine building a house: having many bricks but no wiring or water control does not make a functioning home. A pantry with one ingredient in excess cannot replace every missing ingredient. These comparisons help introduce balanced plant nutrition.

The source calls N the Grower, P the Rooter & Fruiter, and K the Protector. Its house analogy makes N the growing frame, P the foundation and wiring, and K the roof or plumbing. Remember these as prompts for the roles below, not literal one-to-one descriptions. All three participate in several processes; plant growth also depends on the other essential nutrients, light, water and suitable soil conditions.

sourceBindings.text: Nitrogen is part of amino acids and proteins and of chlorophyll, the pigment involved in capturing light for photosynthesis. Adequate N supports leafy and stem growth and a healthy green colour. For a pasture needing more leaf production, N is the nutrient to investigate first in the source example, while the other nutrients and the soil test still matter.

Soil organic matter holds a store of nitrogen. Microorganisms help transform organic N into mineral forms that plants can use; the speed of release depends on conditions. This is one connection in the nutrient cycle, not a promise that organic matter supplies enough N immediately.

An accelerator is a useful memory aid, but flooring it is not a fertilizer recommendation. Too much N can cause excessive soft growth, waste resources and create environmental losses. N, P and K can move from older tissue toward new growth, so shortages often first affect older leaves. That general pattern does not make every older-leaf mark an N, P or K diagnosis: crop, growth stage and other stresses matter. A pale older leaf may prompt a check for N deficiency, but colour alone does not prove the cause. Careful deficiency diagnosis is taught in the step “Evidence-based nutrient symptom interpretation”.

sourceBindings.text: Phosphorus is involved in energy transfer inside the plant. Adequate P supports early root establishment and the processes associated with flowering, fruit and seed development. The source's foundation and power-supply analogy highlights these roles; P does not act alone and does not guarantee flowers or fruit.

Some soil P can be bound to soil constituents and unavailable to roots. Soil pH also changes availability. A soil may therefore contain P without supplying enough to the crop. Conversely, adding more P without evidence can waste money and contribute to nutrient runoff and water enrichment. A diagnosis should consider the soil test, crop stage and field conditions.

sourceBindings.text: Potassium helps regulate water relations and stomatal function and supports stem strength. Unlike N and P, K is not built into the same kind of organic structural compounds; much of its role is regulating plant processes. The source calls it the Protector, but adequate K does not make a crop immune to pests, disease, drought or wind.

Soil K occurs in pools that differ in how quickly they can replenish the soil solution. Total K present is not the same as K immediately available to roots. In the source's windy maize-field example, weak stems and lodging may make K nutrition worth investigating. Wind strength, cultivar, other nutrients, disease and management can also cause lodging, so the observation cannot prove K deficiency by itself.

sourceBindings.text: The three numbers on the source's 10–10–10 fertilizer example are weight percentages in a fixed order: total nitrogen (N), available phosphate expressed as P₂O₅, and soluble potash expressed as K₂O. The label convention reports P and K as oxide equivalents. It does not say that the material contains 10% elemental P and 10% elemental K, or that the bag consists of only those three ingredients.

For a 5 kg bag labelled 10–10–10, the label states 0.5 kg N, 0.5 kg P₂O₅ equivalent and 0.5 kg K₂O equivalent. These values are an arithmetic reading exercise, not a dose or a soil recommendation.
